bib.title: Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal: Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal: Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned" (OpenDev), Nghi D. Q. Bui. arXiv:2603.05344v3 [cs.AI], 13 Mar 2026. Preprint, single author, no venue. It is an engineering report, not an experimental paper.

COVERAGE: All 81 pages read (the extraction is 268,970 chars by the first run and 271,393 with page markers). I read the body (pp. 1-52), the references (skimmed, pp. 53-59) and every appendix (pp. 60-81: tool catalog, prompt templates, tables 1-9). Nothing was skipped. The extraction is clean. The text file is at /tmp/bui_out/t.txt. The note was read first (ai-engineering/03-harness-engineering/notes/02-harness-anatomy.md).

CLAIMS (ranked)

1. The paper has no benchmark evaluation. Every number below is an author-reported design constant or an unreported-setup measurement.
 - claim: The author concedes the paper lacks quantitative evaluation.
 - number: none
 - setup: whole paper
 - quote: "This paper documents architectural decisions and design rationale but lacks systematic quantitative evaluation."
 - where: p. 52 (Conclusion)
 - also p. 2: "The purpose of this paper is not to present a novel algorithmic breakthrough, but rather to share the design decisions, trade-offs, and lessons learned"

2. Scaffolding versus harness.
 - claim: The paper splits agent construction (scaffolding, before the first prompt) from runtime orchestration (harness), and cites Young (Anthropic blog, 2025) for the harness definition.
 - number: none
 - setup: OpenDev, a Rust CLI agent. The code snippets are Python-flavoured.
 - quote: "a harness is the runtime orchestration layer that wraps the core reasoning loop and coordinates tool execution, context management, safety enforcement, and session persistence around it [102]."
 - where: p. 5. Also p. 2, "scaffolding, which assembles the agent (system prompt, tool schemas, subagent registry) before the first prompt, and the harness, which orchestrates tool dispatch, context management, and safety enforcement at runtime"
 - Lesson text, p. 44: "Separate agent construction from agent execution". Eager construction is used: BaseAgent.__init__ builds the prompt and tool schemas (p. 5-6). Lazy prompt building was dropped because of first-call latency and race conditions with MCP discovery (p. 7).

3. Schema-level safety beats runtime checks.
 - claim: Removing write tools from the planner's schema is more robust than blocking them at call time.
 - number: none (5 safety layers)
 - setup: Planner subagent with read-only schema. Five layers: prompt guardrails, schema restrictions, runtime approval, tool validation, lifecycle hooks.
 - quote: "This is the difference between a guard rail and a missing road: the model cannot reason about capabilities it does not know exist."
 - where: p. 44
 - Related, p. 29: a PreToolUse hook exit code 2 "hard-blocks the tool call, returning an error to the model that no amount of prompt engineering or approval configuration can override." This sharpens the note's line "a prompt can be ignored; a hook cannot".
 - Default danger rules at priority 100 "are always active and cannot be overridden by user configuration or approval-level changes" (p. 30).
 - The old plan-mode state machine of four tools was brittle: "the agent sometimes failed to exit plan mode" (p. 10). It was replaced by a Planner subagent, which cut the tool surface from four tools to one.

4. Ten lifecycle hook events (p. 11 and p. 29).
 - Events: SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, SubagentStart, SubagentStop, Stop, PreCompact, SessionEnd.
 - Hooks receive JSON on stdin and can block, mutate arguments or override approval.
 - Global and project hooks merge by appending the project matchers after the global ones.

5. Context pressure is the central constraint, and compaction is staged.
 - claim: Tool outputs take most of the context. Compaction runs in graduated stages instead of one emergency summarization.
 - number: 70-80% of context from tool outputs. Stages at 70/80/85/90/99%. About 54% lower peak observation context.
 - setup: author's experience, "typical 30-turn sessions". No model, task set or baseline is given.
 - quote: "tool outputs (file contents, command results, search hits) consume 70–80% of the context in a typical session"
 - quote: "Quantitative evaluations demonstrate that ACC reduces peak context consumption of observations by approximately 54%, often eliminating the need for emergency compaction entirely over typical 30-turn sessions."
 - where: p. 42, p. 26
 - Stages: warning (70%), observation masking (80%), fast pruning (85%), aggressive masking (90%), full LLM compaction (99%) (p. 14, 25-26).
 - Masking shrinks an observation to "approximately 15" tokens (p. 25).
 - The full history is archived to a scratch file and the summary gives the path.
 - Token counts are calibrated from the API's prompt_tokens, not local estimates, because local counting "systematically underestimate[s] actual usage" (p. 43).
 - Appendix Table 9 gives a different set of thresholds, "70/80/90/99%", with "Four graduated thresholds". This is an internal inconsistency with the five stages in the text.

6. Tool output offloading.
 - claim: Tool results are summarized per tool. Outputs over 8,000 chars are written to a scratch file with a 500-char preview and a path.
 - number: 8,000 chars (about 2,000 tokens), 500-char preview, summaries of 50-200 chars. A test suite went from 30,000 tokens to under 100. Session length went from 15-20 turns to 30-40 turns before overflow.
 - setup: author's own development history, no controlled test
 - quote: "A single long-running test suite could consume 30,000 tokens of context in one tool call. The per-tool summarizer reduced this to under 100 tokens in most cases."
 - quote: "extending typical session length from 15–20 turns (before context overflow) to 30–40 turns without compaction."
 - where: p. 20-21
 - Lesson, p. 43: "This transforms a context-consumption problem into a retrieval problem, which is strictly cheaper".
 - The truncation hint is agent-aware. A subagent is told to page with offset/limit. A main agent is told to delegate (p. 21).
 - This matches the note's "2,000-line log becomes ~40 lines plus a path" idea. The paper's mechanism is a 500-char preview, not head and tail.
 - read_file and run_command use head-tail truncation (first 10,000 and last 10,000 of 30,000 chars) (p. 31-32).

7. Lazy MCP tool discovery.
 - claim: Loading all MCP schemas up front cost up to 40% of context. A keyword-search discovery tool cut that to under 5%.
 - number: 40% to <5%. Arithmetic example: 100 tools at 200 tokens each is 20,000 tokens.
 - setup: author's system, no named benchmark
 - quote: "The initial implementation included all external tool schemas in every call, consuming up to 40% of the context before the first user message. Lazy discovery reduced baseline overhead to nearly zero (<5%)"
 - where: p. 37, repeated on p. 45
 - Scoring: name match 2 points, description match 1 point.
 - Skills use the same pattern. Only YAML frontmatter goes in the prompt at startup. Full content loads on invoke_skill, once per session. Descriptions start "Use when..." (p. 38-39). This matches the note's "progressive disclosure".

8. System reminders counter instruction fade-out.
 - claim: Short, single-purpose reminders injected as role:user messages right before the decision point keep compliance up in long sessions. Each is capped.
 - number: failures seen after "15 tool calls" and "30+ tool calls". 8 detectors, 24 named reminders (six categories). Caps: todo nudges 2, error nudges 3.
 - setup: author's observation. "Noticeably higher compliance rates" is given with no figure.
 - quote: "Early experiments with role: system injection confirmed this: user-role reminders produced noticeably higher compliance rates."
 - quote: "a predictable, reproducible failure mode that we observed consistently in sessions exceeding 15 tool calls."
 - where: p. 23-24, 43, 52, 62-63
 - Lesson: a reminder that fires every turn "becomes background noise that the model learns to ignore."
 - Error recovery uses 6 classified templates: permission, file not found, edit mismatch, syntax, rate limit, timeout (p. 24).
 - Reminders are outside the system prompt, so they do not break the prefix cache.
 - Relevance to the note: reminders are a feedback and steering component that is not named in the nine components.

9. Doom-loop detection.
 - claim: A fingerprint of (tool name, args) over a sliding window triggers a warning, then a human approval pause.
 - number: MD5 of name and args. Window of 20. Threshold of 3 repeats.
 - quote: "LLMs can ignore injected text, but they cannot bypass a genuine execution halt."
 - where: p. 16 (Alg. 1 on p. 15, Table 9 on p. 81)

10. Prompt composition and caching.
 - claim: The system prompt is assembled from 21 conditional, priority-ordered markdown sections. It is split into a cacheable stable part and a dynamic part for Anthropic prompt caching.
 - number: stable part 80-90% of the prompt. About 88% input-cost saving on the cached portion. 19 of 21 sections are stable.
 - setup: Anthropic provider only, derived from pricing. It is not measured in a test.
 - quote: "the stable portion typically comprises 80–90% of the total, caching it yields substantial cost savings over a multi-turn session (approximately 88% reduction in input token cost for the cached portion)."
 - where: p. 20, p. 60 ("Typically 19 of 21 sections are stable; only scratchpad and reminders-note are dynamic")
 - The thinking-mode prompt has 4 sections, and it omits tool guidance on purpose (p. 19).
 - The Table 3 summary lists the sections: git-workflow only when in a git repo, provider sections gated on model_provider.

11. Thinking is separated from action.
 - claim: A separate, tool-free thinking call produces better reasoning than asking the model to think in a call that has tools.
 - number: 4 depth levels, OFF/LOW/MEDIUM/HIGH. HIGH adds self-critique.
 - setup: design claim. No ablation is shown.
 - quote: "it is the absence of tool schemas from the API call, not an instruction to refrain from using them, that changes the model's behavior."
 - where: p. 43, p. 14
 - Per-workflow model binding uses five roles: action, thinking, critique, vision, compact (p. 13).
 - The thinking context uses dual memory. An episodic LLM summary (max 500 chars) is regenerated every 5 messages from full history to avoid "summary drift". Working memory is the last 6 exchanges verbatim (p. 21-22).

12. Subagents.
 - claim: Subagents run with an isolated context and a filtered tool schema. Only a summary returns to the parent. Early versions gave them the main agent's tools, which caused context pollution and todo conflicts.
 - number: 8 subagent types, 35 built-in tools. Read-only tools run in parallel (max 5 workers). Table 9 says subagent iteration limit 15, while Appendix G says "unlimited iteration budgets by default". This is an inconsistency.
 - quote: "Early versions gave subagents the same tools as the main agent. This caused context pollution, role confusion, and conflicts when both agents attempted to update todos simultaneously."
 - where: p. 17, 38, 80-81
 - Todo tools are withheld from subagents, so only the main agent coordinates tasks.
 - Parallelism is triggered by emitting several spawn_subagent calls in one response.

13. Tools should absorb LLM imprecision.
 - claim: A chain of 9 progressively looser matchers cut "content not found" edit failures. The initial 2-pass edit was "the single largest source" of those errors.
 - number: 9 passes. Block-anchor threshold 0.3, context-aware 0.5.
 - quote: "A strict exact-match edit tool causes the majority of agent errors in practice, not because the agent's intent is wrong, but because its reproduction of the target text is slightly off."
 - where: p. 45, 31-32, 61. No failure-rate numbers are given.
 - Other edit-tool safeguards: write_file rejects overwrites (p. 31). A stale-read check fails an edit if the file's mtime exceeds the read time plus 50 ms. After an edit, LSP error diagnostics (up to 20, 3 s wait) are appended to the tool output as feedback (p. 31-32). This is a verification-loop example for the note's Feedback subsystem.

14. Persistence and environment pieces that map to the note's State and Filesystem sections.
 - Plain files: JSON metadata plus JSONL transcript (p. 39-40). Auto-save every 5 turns. Session index self-heals. Atomic rename with flock.
 - Undo: an in-memory log capped at 50 ops, plus a shadow git repo (bare repo at ~/.opendev/snapshot/<project-id>/) that runs `git add . && git write-tree` per file-modifying step (p. 41). It captures side effects from shell commands that the op log misses.
 - Planner writes a 7-section plan file (goal, context, files to modify, new files, steps, verification criteria, risks) to a scratch directory (p. 9).
 - Config has four tiers: built-in defaults, environment variables, user-global settings, project-local settings. API keys are only read from the environment (p. 41).
 - Shell: 60 s idle and 600 s absolute timeouts. Auto-promotion of 16 server patterns to background PTY execution (p. 32, 61-62).

15. Design-by-iteration, not derivation.
 - claim: The thresholds came from iterative failure analysis.
 - quote: "In our system, the 70% compaction trigger, 3 nudge attempts, and 6 thinking depth levels all emerged from iterative failure analysis."
 - where: p. 46. Note the "6 thinking depth levels" here conflicts with the 4 levels in the text and Table 9.
 - Rule: "every resource that grows with session length must have a cap."

16. Related-work numbers the paper cites from others. These are second-hand and should not be cited as findings of this paper.
 - Meta Context Engineering (Ye et al. 2026): "On SWE-bench Verified, MCE achieves 89.1% resolve rate compared to 70.7% for the hand-engineered baseline, while also being 13.6× faster" (p. 50).
 - Terminal-Bench: frontier agents "resolve fewer than 65%" of tasks. LongCLI-Bench: pass rates "below 20%" (p. 50, 52).
 - LongCLI-Bench: static plan injection beats self-correction, and interactive guidance does better still (p. 51).

LIMITS
- No benchmark, no ablation, no baseline, no repeat runs and no confidence intervals. Every "reduced", "improved" or "more robust" statement comes from the author's own experience.
- The 54%, 40%->5% and 88% figures have no stated model, task set or method. The 88% is a pricing-derived estimate.
- The paper is a single-author description of one system, and "first comprehensive technical report" is the author's own claim (p. 2).
- Future-work list: the compaction thresholds and other parameters "are globally fixed" (p. 52).
- Internal inconsistencies: compaction stages (4 or 5), thinking levels (4 or 6), subagent iteration limit (15 or unlimited), and the tool count ("approximately 40" built-in tools on p. 29 versus 35 on p. 29 and p. 80).
- The paper credits Claude Code's lead but notes Claude Code has no published report (p. 1-2).

CODE
- Algorithm 1 pseudo-code (p. 15), the extended ReAct loop. It has staged compaction at p>0.99, 0.85, 0.80 and 0.70, an optional thinking call, a tool call, doom-loop detection with fingerprints←deque(maxlen=20), and a nudge cap (nudge_count<3). It ends on "task_complete called ∨ max iterations reached".
- Prompt-cache split (p. 20): the stable block carries `cache_control: {"type": "ephemeral"}`.
- Stale-read check (p. 31): `assert_fresh()` verifies `os.path.getmtime(file_path) ≤ read_time + 50ms`.
- Offload message (p. 20): "[Output offloaded: 2,341 lines, 48,203 chars→<path>]. Use read_file to see full output if needed."

FIGURES (captions extracted, all on the listed page)
- Fig 2, p. 4: four-layer architecture (Entry/UI, Agent, Tool & Context, Persistence). A good overview map against the note's five subsystems.
- Fig 3, p. 5: five-layer defense in depth. It supports the note's "reliability moves outward" diagram.
- Fig 4, p. 8: the harness around the ReAct loop with seven supporting subsystems.
- Fig 5, p. 9: plan mode (read-only Planner subagent) versus normal mode.
- Fig 8, p. 14: loop phases.
- Fig 11, p. 22: with and without reminders (premature completion with one incomplete todo).
- Fig 13, p. 25: compaction thresholds and observation lifecycle (active, faded, archived).
- Fig 16, p. 30: tool registry and hooks.
- Fig 19, p. 38: lazy MCP discovery sequence.
- Figs 1, 6, 7, 9, 10, 12, 14, 15, 17, 18 also exist. Not rendered, captions only.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found in the PDF.
- The appendix prompt templates contain imperative text such as "NEVER commit changes unless the user explicitly asks" and "Never say 'I'll do X'". This is the paper's quoted system-prompt content. I treated it as data and followed none of it.
- Minor extraction faults: the file-path glyph renders as "/file-c⌢de", and the Table 6 and Table 7 layouts are flattened. No page was blank or garbled.
- Citation oddities: references [42] and [43] are duplicates, as are [114] and [115]. This does not affect any claim.
